common_name: Viking 204 BMR Sorghum-Sudangrass (Multi-Cut Brown Midrib Forage and Cover Crop Hybrid)
scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor × Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense 'Viking 204'

planting.note: Direct sow from late spring into early summer once soil is reliably above 62°F; Viking 204 is bred for short northern growing seasons and multiple cuttings rather than a single tall harvest.

directions: Viking 204 is a brown-midrib sorghum-sudangrass hybrid selected for a shorter, faster-maturing frame than tall silage-type sorghums, making it well suited to shorter northern summers where growers still want two or three forage cuts. The BMR trait lowers lignin content in the leaves and stems, so regrowth after mowing stays leafier and more digestible than a standard-lignin sudangrass. Drill or broadcast into warm soil after the last frost, then mow around 40 inches tall or roughly 45 to 55 days after seeding to trigger vigorous tillering rather than letting the crop bolt to full height. As with other sorghum-sudangrass types, avoid grazing or feeding fresh-cut regrowth immediately after a frost or drought stress, since prussic acid can accumulate in stressed young tissue.
sources: University of Kentucky Grain and Forage Crops Extension

common_name: Prime 180 BMR Hybrid Pearl Millet (Dwarf Leafy Forage and Cover Crop Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past the last frost; Prime 180 is a dwarf brown midrib pearl millet bred to stay short and leafy rather than growing tall like standard pearl millet.

directions: Prime 180 is a dwarf, leafy brown midrib pearl millet hybrid bred for a shorter, sturdier stand than standard tall pearl millet, which reduces lodging and keeps more of the plant's mass in easily grazed or cut leaf tissue. Its compact height and strong standability let it hold up under repeated grazing or hay cutting through the warm season while still shading soil and adding organic matter between cash crops. Sow into warm, moist soil well after the last frost, since pearl millet germinates poorly in cool ground, and clip or graze before seed heads mature to keep regrowth vigorous. Unlike sorghum-sudangrass, pearl millet carries no prussic acid risk, so frost-stressed or drought-stressed regrowth can be grazed without that particular caution.

common_name: Maxi Pearl Millet (Tall Warm-Season Forage and Cover Crop Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past the last frost; Maxi grows into one of the tallest millets, so give it the full summer growing window before a killing frost.

directions: Maxi is among the tallest pearl millet types sold for forage and cover cropping, capable of reaching 7 to 8 feet with woody, upright stems and long pointed leaf blades. Its height and vigorous warm-season growth make it a heavy biomass producer for building organic matter or screening out weeds over a full summer fallow window, though the stand should be grazed or mowed starting around 24 to 30 inches to keep it from becoming too fibrous. Direct sow into warm soil once frost danger has passed, since germination slows sharply in cool ground, and allow adequate regrowth time if grazing down to a 6-inch stubble. A hard freeze terminates the stand cleanly, leaving substantial residue to break down before the next planting.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Georgia Forages

common_name: Sodbuster Forage Radish (New Zealand-Origin Deep-Tillage Daikon-Type Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in late summer, roughly 6 to 10 weeks before the first fall frost, so the taproot has time to drive deep before winter kill.

directions: Sodbuster is a large-rooted daikon-type forage radish that originated in New Zealand as a farmer selection rather than a formal breeding program, and it has since become a widely traded tillage-radish option in North American cover crop mixes. Its long, thick taproot can drive several feet down through compacted layers, opening physical channels for water and root growth in the following cash crop. Drill or broadcast in late summer so plants build a full rosette and root mass before a hard freeze, since the crop is grown specifically to winterkill and leave an easily worked seedbed by spring. The decomposing root also releases scavenged nitrogen and organic matter back into the topsoil as it breaks down over the following weeks.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Escambia County
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center, Big Flats, NY

common_name: Colonel Oilseed Radish (European-Bred Branching-Root Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6 to 10 weeks before the first fall frost into a well-prepared seedbed; Colonel builds a branched, stubbier root system rather than one long daikon-type taproot.

directions: Colonel is a European-bred oilseed radish cultivar selected for a stubbier, more branched taproot than daikon-type tillage radishes, trading some single-channel depth for a wider network of smaller roots and generally greater winter hardiness. Drill or broadcast into a firm seedbed in late summer so the rosette establishes well before frost, since it is grown to scavenge nitrogen and build biomass quickly rather than to overwinter. The dense top growth suppresses fall weeds and the fibrous root mass leaves the surface soil looser and easier to work by spring in most temperate climates. Like other oilseed radish types, decomposing residue after a hard freeze can produce a strong sulfurous odor for a week or two, which is a normal part of the breakdown process.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Bulletin E2907

common_name: Adagio Oilseed Radish (European Biofumigant Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6 to 10 weeks before the first fall frost; Adagio has performed comparably to other oilseed types in university trials for total biomass production.

directions: Adagio is one of several European oilseed radish cultivars imported for North American cover crop use, alongside types like Colonel and Remonta, and in Michigan field trials it produced total dry biomass comparable to those other named selections, often exceeding four tons per acre. It shares the fast-growing, high-glucosinolate character of the oilseed radish group, sending up a broad leaf rosette over a shorter, more branched root than a daikon-type tillage radish. Broadcast or drill into a firm seedbed in late summer so the crop has time to build biomass and scavenge residual nitrogen before a killing frost ends growth for the season. In milder winter regions the rosette can persist and bolt the following spring, so mow before flowering if a volunteer seed bank is unwanted.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Bulletin E2907
PMC (National Library of Medicine) — Oilseed Radish Cultivar Susceptibility Study

common_name: Kaspa Field Pea (Semi-Leafless Dun-Type Grain and Cover Crop Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring in cold-winter climates, or in fall in mild-winter Mediterranean-type climates; Kaspa's semi-leafless, tendril-heavy habit keeps the crop standing better than older trailing field pea types.

directions: Kaspa was released in the early 2000s as a semi-dwarf, semi-leafless dun-type field pea and quickly became a dominant cultivar across southeastern and Western Australian cropping regions because of its shatter-resistant pods and improved standing ability. Its leaflets are largely replaced by branching tendrils, so plants hook together into a self-supporting mat that resists lodging far better than older trailing-type field peas, which simplifies both mechanical harvest and cover crop termination. Drill inoculated seed into cool, workable soil, since it germinates and grows well at cooler spring or autumn temperatures. Whether grown through to dry grain or terminated earlier as a nitrogen-fixing green manure, the tendrilled canopy also forms a dense residual mulch that suppresses weeds while it breaks down.
sources: Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Western Australia
